title: Ang 220–242: Gauri ashtpadis
tomorrow: who is the bride in Gauri's wedding songs?

cards: Open one tab to study. Ten minutes later there are eleven, and none of them is the one you opened.
Simran had the driver's handbook propped on her knees last night, and her mind was everywhere else: the cone video, the pickup, a song stuck on repeat.
The longer hymns of Gauri, which start on Ang 220, have a picture for a mind like that. It's an elephant.

teach.b: The question is old: how do you steer a mind that won't listen?

Guru Nanak answers in a Gauri ashtpadi on Ang 221, in paraphrase: the mind is an elephant, loose in the forest of the body; the Guru is the goad, and the true Word is the mark it follows; at the King's gate, it finds honor.
An elephant isn't wicked. It's huge, strong and easily spooked, and when it's loose it tramples the garden. The goad doesn't fight that strength.
It turns it. Something to tell a friend tonight: another path uses the same animal.

The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, says in Max Müller's translation: "This mind of mine went formerly wandering about as it liked, as it listed, as it pleased; but I shall now hold it in thoroughly, as the rider who holds the hook holds in the furious elephant."
Two paths, one picture: the mind as an elephant, steered by a hook.
And one honest difference. In the Dhammapada, the rider holds the hook; the steering is the practitioner's own resolve.
In Guru Nanak's hymn, the goad is the Guru and the mark is the Word; the steering comes through the Guru. Neither is the other. Both know the elephant.

how: Gauri's longer hymns, headed ashtpadis, are read in the Granth's order and sung as kirtan; Sikhs speak of steering the mind by the Guru's Word, and Buddhists read the Dhammapada's elephant verses as a teaching on training the mind.

games.q: a friend who reads Buddhist writing says the Dhammapada has a mind-as-elephant verse. she asks if the Sikh hymn says the same thing. what's fair?
o: same picture, honest difference: there the rider holds the hook; here the Guru is the goad.
exactly the same teaching, just in two languages.
nothing alike: one is about a horse, the other an elephant.
games.why: both picture the mind as an elephant and a hook that steers it. in the Dhammapada the rider steers; in Guru Nanak's hymn the steering comes through the Guru and the Word.

practice: Close your eyes and let the mind go where it goes. Each time you notice it has wandered into a tab, a clip or a worry, turn it gently back to the breath, the way a goad turns an elephant: no fight, just a touch.
Count the turns if it helps; the turning is the practice.
